features.title: Write and edit notes
features.summary: Write a note, change it, add to the top or bottom of it, and throw it away. Deleting puts a note in the Trash, which is somewhere you can look and take things back out of rather than a countdown — nothing is destroyed until you empty it.
gui: Create a note in a notebook — executed (new-note-in-notebook)
Edit and save a note — executed (edit-save)
Restore a note from Trash — executed (trash-restore)
Move this note to the Trash
Permanently delete this note and its revisions
features.surface_note: All four surfaces write notes. At a terminal, `notes create` takes a body from a file or a pipe, so a note can be the end of a pipeline, and `notes append` and `notes prepend` add to a note without rewriting it — which matters because no surface can patch a range of a body. Deleting and restoring are deliberately on the same surface: a delete whose undo lives somewhere else is a poor boundary.

features.title: Read a note and its structure
features.summary: Open a note whole, or take just the part you need: the body, an outline of its headings, one of its blocks, a range of lines, or an earlier revision. The structured views exist so a program can work on part of a note without parsing the rest.
features.surface_note: The command line prints a note as Markdown with front matter, so another application can read it as a file, and `--json` gives the fields instead; `notes outline`, `notes resources` and `notes links` answer what a note is made of. Blocks, line ranges and revisions are on REST and MCP only — they are for programs working inside a note, and a terminal has `notes show` and a text editor.

features.title: Search your notes
features.summary: Find notes by text, tag, notebook, date and the rest of the query language — one language, whether you type it into the search box or hand it to a command. You can search a whole library or inside a single note.
features.surface_note: A search is what turns a question into something you can act on: every hit carries the note's identifier, which is what `notes show`, `notes move`, `tags add` and the batch operations take. `--count` answers how many without paging through them, and `--links` prints the `notrios://` form for pasting into another machine's library. A search spans every collection unless `collection:` narrows it, and leaves the Trash out unless the query says `is:trashed`.

features.title: Notebooks that are really saved searches
features.summary: Save a query as a notebook, so a view you would otherwise retype becomes something you open.
features.surface_note: At a terminal this is `notebooks create --query`. In the interface it is offered on a search that has already run and returned something, rather than as a form to fill in: a notebook built from a query nobody has watched work opens empty as easily as it opens right. The query is shown and is not editable there, which is what keeps it from becoming a second search box.
gui: Keep this search — an action on a search that has run

features.title: Organise notes into notebooks
features.summary: Make notebooks, nest them inside each other, move notes between them, and see what deleting a notebook would take with it before you agree to it.
gui: Choose a notebook for a new note — executed (new-note-in-notebook)
features.surface_note: `notebooks list` prints a table of names and identifiers, with `--json` for the structured form — the identifier is what a query and the note commands take, so finding it should not mean reading a JSON object at a terminal. Deleting a notebook shows what it holds first, on every surface that offers it.

features.title: Tag and untag a note
features.summary: Put a tag on a note, take one off, and see what a note carries. Tags are hierarchical: `field/dusk` sits under `field`, and a search for `field` finds both.

features.title: See and rename tags
features.summary: See the tags a library uses, ask whether one exists, and rename a tag — or a whole branch of them — everywhere at once.
features.surface_note: `tags show` exits non-zero when a tag does not exist, so a script can test for one without parsing anything, and `--prefix` asks for one branch of the hierarchy rather than the whole vocabulary. A rename shows what it would change before it changes it, and a change described as a merge means the destination already exists and the two tags become one. Listing the notes that carry a tag is a search — `tag:todo` — rather than a second thing this reports.
gui: Tags in the sidebar with note counts
Rename the tag — beside each tag
Show me what changes — the dry run
Rename — applies what the report described

features.title: See where notes came from
features.summary: Notes you import stay marked with where they came from, so material brought in from somewhere else is distinguishable from what you wrote yourself — and you can search within one source or across all of them.
features.surface_note: A collection is provenance rather than a place notes live: an import files notes into a notebook, which is what you browse, and marks them with a collection identifier alongside. A search spans every collection and `collection:` narrows it to one; `notriosctl collections list` says which exist and how many notes name each. Collections are made by an import naming one rather than by a command of their own, and the note inspector shows the row only when a note came from somewhere, because printing `default` on everything you wrote here would say nothing. A collection's name and description can be edited over REST, since renaming a label changes no provenance.
gui: Collection — shown in the note inspector when a note came from somewhere

features.title: Attach and manage files
features.summary: Attach files to notes, read them back out, see what references what, and find attachments nothing points at any more.
features.surface_note: Where the link goes in your prose is yours, and the two surfaces differ because only one of them knows where you are typing. In the interface, attaching a file inserts the Markdown at the cursor and leaves the note unsaved. At a terminal, `resources add` puts the file in the library and prints its `resource://` URI without touching the body; `notes append` or `notes prepend` place it once you have decided where it belongs. The bytes are stored once and addressed by their content, so the same file attached twice is stored once.
gui: Upload image/PDF/resource — the file field in the note inspector

features.title: Bring remote images into the library
features.summary: A note that points at an image on somebody else's server stops working when that server does. Find those images, see what the policy decided about each one, and copy the allowed ones in so the note stops depending on anyone.
features.surface_note: Localizing is offered where you are editing, because it rewrites the note. It is deliberately not a general downloader: every fetch goes through the domain policy, quarantine, hashing and size limits, so a note cannot be made to pull an arbitrary address into your library. The scan that lists them downloads nothing — each decision is made from the address alone.
gui: Remote media list — shown on a note that points at images on the web

features.title: Link notes to each other
features.summary: Get a stable link to a note or to one of its sections, follow one, check that a draft's links still resolve before you save it, and register Notrios as the program that opens `notrios://` links.
gui: Insert a link and check it — executed (insert-and-check-link)

features.title: See the shape of the link graph
features.summary: See what surrounds a note, find the path between two of them, and get a report on the notes nothing links to, the ones that link to nothing, and the few that everything runs through.

features.title: Templates and tasks
features.summary: Keep notes that are shapes for other notes, make new ones from them, and see the tasks scattered across a library in one list.
features.surface_note: Both are ordinary Markdown rather than tables in a database: a template is a note carrying a note-template block, and a task is a checkbox line in a note tagged `task` or `todo`. So nothing creates a task — writing `- [ ] chase the permit` in a note is how one comes to exist — and what the command line adds is the other half: asking what remains, and filling in a template. A placeholder you leave out is refused rather than quietly left blank, so a template that gains a field fails the scripts that do not know about it. The tag is required because a checkbox is ordinary Markdown and turns up in quoted examples; `--untagged` asks for those too. Not in the interface yet.

features.title: Live query blocks inside a note
features.summary: Put a query inside a note and have its results render where it sits, so a note can show what currently matches instead of a list somebody has to keep up to date.
features.surface_note: A query block is a rendering rather than a command: the note carries a fenced query and the interface shows what it matches in place, which is a line rather than a gap. At a terminal the same question is `notriosctl search`, and formatting the answer is a template tool's job. A command that ran a block's query would be a second way to run a query.
gui: Query blocks render in the preview, in place

features.title: Reorganise many notes at once
features.summary: Reorganise a lot of notes in one go: move, tag, untag, duplicate, trash or restore everything a search finds, as one reviewable action.
features.surface_note: At a terminal the set is named by a search rather than by a list of identifiers: `--query` on `notes move`, `notes delete`, `notes restore`, `notes duplicate`, `tags add` and `tags remove`. Nothing happens until you add `--apply` — without it the command shows the notes it would act on and stops — and a selection larger than the 500-note ceiling is refused rather than trimmed, because acting on the first five hundred of a thousand matches looks exactly like success. Over REST and MCP the same run takes an explicit list and a request key that makes a retry safe. Selecting several notes in the interface is not built yet.

features.title: Import from another application
features.summary: Bring in what you already have elsewhere: a Joplin export, an Obsidian vault, a Twitter or X archive, a ChatGPT or Claude export, or another Notrios archive. Every importer shows you what it would do before it does it.
features.surface_note: Importing names a folder on the machine running the library, so it belongs to the desktop application and the command line and has no REST route at all; in a browser the control is shown and disabled with that reason rather than hidden. The desktop application handles Joplin, Obsidian and Notrios archives, and merges only — replace, fork and adopt stay at the command line because they change which library this is. Twitter, ChatGPT and Claude imports are command line only.

features.title: Export your library
features.summary: Write a portable archive of the whole library or a chosen part of it, check one against this version before trusting it, verify one, and restore one when you mean to.
features.surface_note: Exporting names a folder on the machine running the library, so it belongs to the desktop application and the command line and has no REST route; in a browser the control is shown and disabled with that reason. The interface writes a complete archive; choosing a subset by notebook, tag or query stays at the command line, because choosing a subset means seeing what it selects first.

features.title: Back up and restore the whole library
features.summary: Take a copy of everything — the database, the attachments and the history — check that it is sound, and put it back later, either over this library or as a new replica beside it.
features.surface_note: Snapshots name a folder on the machine running the library, so they are desktop and command line only. Taking one is in the interface; restoring one is not, because a restore replaces the library the window is showing. Restoring asks which you mean — replace this library, or adopt the snapshot as a separate replica — rather than choosing for you.

features.title: Pair two of your own libraries
features.summary: Teach two of your own libraries to trust each other: enrol one, issue a single-use code, and spend it from the other side.
features.surface_note: No MCP tools, deliberately: an assistant can watch a synchronization run and cannot decide who is trusted. Pairing also reads and writes files you name, which is why it has no general REST route either. Pairing from a phone would go through the shared library rather than through MCP, and that surface carries no synchronization yet.

features.title: Synchronize with a replica
features.summary: Exchange changes with a library you have paired: directly over an authenticated connection, or through a folder you can both reach — a second drive, or a cloud folder mapped into this machine.

features.title: See and end trust between replicas
features.summary: See which replicas a library trusts, take one's key away, and retire a peer once you have read exactly what retiring it means.
features.surface_note: No MCP tools, under the same rule as pairing: an assistant can watch a synchronization and cannot decide who is trusted. Retiring a peer is a permanent identity decision recorded with a signature, and revoking a key with `--advance-epoch` changes what every other replica will accept — both show you what they mean before they happen.

features.title: Recover a replica and resolve conflicts
features.summary: When a replica is lost, or two of them disagree: fetch a backup a peer has verified, look inside one without installing it, work through the conflicts a synchronization could not settle, and decide what a shared attachment should do.

features.title: Choose where sync keys are kept
features.summary: An installed Notrios keeps the key protecting your sync material in the operating system's credential store. Move existing keys between that and the owner-only development file, in either direction.
features.surface_note: Credentials are managed from the command line and nowhere else, firmly: a remote route that can move a key is a remote route that can take one. An installed Notrios never silently falls back to a plaintext file, and nothing here prints, logs or exports a secret.

features.title: Watch and steer long-running work
features.summary: Imports, exports and synchronizations run as jobs rather than as a window you have to keep open. List them, look at one, cancel it, retry it, or reset one that is stuck.
features.surface_note: The interface has the sync centre's list of recent synchronization jobs, with Cancel on one still running and Retry on one that failed or was cancelled — a retry resumes from the last verified checkpoint rather than from the beginning. Import, export and snapshot jobs do not appear there, and there is no general job list, no inspect and no reset in the interface yet; the command line, REST and MCP have all of it.
gui: Recent synchronization jobs — kind, state and progress
Cancel — while a sync job is running or queued
Retry — on a sync job that failed or was cancelled

features.title: Keep separate libraries
features.summary: Run more than one library on a machine — personal notes, work notes, a blog — each with its own database, its own settings and its own address.
features.surface_note: Switching between profiles is in the interface; making, registering and forgetting them is command-line work, and a browser cannot manage them at all. The absence from REST and MCP is deliberate rather than unfinished: `profile create` names a directory to keep a library in and `profile start` launches a process, so a route that accepted those would let a caller point the service at any directory and start something.
gui: Active profile — the selector in the sync centre's Setup tab

features.title: Publish a subset of your notes
features.summary: Publish a chosen part of your library and nothing else. Review exactly what would be included and what would be held back, save that choice as a profile, and publish only after agreeing to the plan you were shown.
features.surface_note: The review is the feature rather than a step before it, so it is in the interface, and the counts lead with what is withheld and which links get rewritten rather than with what is sent. `publish run` re-plans and refuses unless what it computes still matches what you reviewed. Profiles are read here and never written: a profile carries a target, a selection and a privacy policy, and a form that quietly defaulted one is how something private gets published, so authoring stays `notriosctl publish profile save`.
gui: Publish a subset of your notes — choosing a saved profile
Publish this review — in the desktop application only

features.title: Keep a library healthy
features.summary: Find what has rotted — broken links, attachments nothing points at, notes referring to things that are gone — fix what can be fixed mechanically, reclaim the space, and check that this installation is set up the way you think it is.
features.surface_note: Reporting and repairing are in the interface and at the command line. Over REST the lint surface is read-only on purpose: that is the surface a program reaches, and repairs to somebody's notes should not be one call away from one. Every repair writes a revision against the revision it was planned on, so a note edited in between is refused rather than repaired against text nobody read. Reclaiming space stays `notriosctl gc --apply`, because it deletes blobs and there is no revision to go back to. `doctor`, `paths` and `config show` are command line only.
gui: Health — the lint report and the collection plan
Show me what would be repaired
Repair them — in the desktop application only

features.title: Move a pre-0.8 library into place
features.summary: A library that lived in a `./data` folder next to the program moves into the directories an installed Notrios uses — after showing you the plan.
features.surface_note: This one is genuinely command-line work: it relocates the directories the running program is using, which is not something a program can sensibly do to itself while serving them.

features.title: Let an AI assistant use your library
features.summary: Notrios speaks MCP, so an assistant can read your library and, within a scope you grant, change it. What it may touch is yours to decide, and establishing trust between replicas and managing credentials are outside every scope.
features.surface_note: This is a surface Notrios serves rather than something you run: software with an MCP client connects to it, so there is nothing to demonstrate at a terminal or in a window — a journey would document the client rather than this program. The two REST operations listed here are how the endpoint is reached.
